name: Japanese court paper-forming regulations
description: The Engishiki contains paper-production provisions that later researchers interpret alongside surviving Japanese documents as evidence of mucilage-assisted hand sheet forming.

impact.note: Court regulations witnessing an improved sheet-forming method in the court's own mill; wider Japanese papermaking is not shown to descend from this text.

date.label: 927 submission to 967 implementation of revised regulations
date.basis: Date of the stated witness or contextual sample, not a claim of global origin.

events.statement: The Engishiki contains paper-production provisions that later researchers interpret alongside surviving Japanese documents as evidence of mucilage-assisted hand sheet forming.

evidence.supports: Yuyama describes Engishiki rules specifying 20,000 annual sheets and proposes that ancient Japanese papers used plant-derived neri and a tamezuki-like nagashizuki process. These are rules and scholarly reconstruction, not directly measured historical output.
The Engishiki was submitted in 927, revised and brought into effect in 967, according to Kokugakuin University. This establishes a textual timeline, not actual papermaking output.

events.caveats: The 927 date is submission of the Engishiki and 967 its later implementation following revision; the 20,000-sheet figure is a regulation, not measured annual production. The specific forming technique is a modern reconstruction from historical texts and papers, not a demonstrated universal origin or exact date of invention.
